datasets.title: Global Sea Surface Temperature
datasets.description: Ocean currents around the world from March 2007 to March 2008, coloured by how warm the surface water is. The warmest water, around 28 to 30 degrees Celsius, forms a wide band along the equator, and the water cools steadily toward the poles, down to about 0 degrees. The pattern changes slowly, warming in the north during the northern summer and in the south during the southern summer.
datasets.colorMeaning: blue = cold (0°C), green = mild, yellow = warm, red = hot (32°C)
datasets.credit: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio

datasets.title: Change in Night Lights 2012–2023
datasets.description: Earth at night, seen from space by the Suomi NPP satellite, one picture for each year from 2012 to 2023. The oceans and most of the land are dark, and city lights shine where people live: the eastern United States, Europe, India, China and Japan are the brightest. Each year is shown for two and a half seconds, and the lights slowly spread and grow brighter. Comparing 2012 with 2023, lights grew most across China, India, Southeast Asia and the Middle East, while parts of Western Europe, such as the United Kingdom and France, became a little dimmer.
datasets.colorMeaning: yellow and white = city lights (brighter = more light), black = ocean or unlit land; the background map shows grey snow and ice and brown deserts
datasets.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio. Data: NASA Black Marble (Suomi NPP VIIRS)

datasets.title: Lightning Events Detected from the ISS 2017–2023
datasets.description: Lightning flashes detected from space by an instrument on the International Space Station, from about 2017 to 2023. Each flash appears as a small yellow dot that stays for a moment and then disappears, so the map shows the last ten days of lightning as time moves forward. Most lightning strikes over land in the tropics, especially in central Africa, South America and Southeast Asia. Storm activity swells once a year, during each northern summer, when storms spread across North America, Europe and Asia. The station only sees between about 52 degrees north and south, so the far north and south stay empty.
datasets.colorMeaning: yellow dots = lightning flashes from the last ten days; the grey map shows land and country borders, and the darker bands at the top and bottom are areas the space station cannot see
datasets.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio. Data: Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS) on the International Space Station

datasets.title: DYAMOND Global Carbon Dioxide
datasets.description: A computer model of carbon dioxide in the air, shown on a turning globe from 14 January to 3 March 2020. The camera slowly travels westward around the Earth: it starts over East Asia and Australia, passes India and the Indian Ocean, then Africa, crosses the Atlantic Ocean and ends over South America. Orange and red patches show where carbon dioxide near the ground is highest, mostly over the forests of central Africa and the Amazon, and over East Asia. These patches pulse once every model day, building up at night and fading in the daytime, which looks like a quick flicker in the video. The sound follows what is facing you on the globe, so it changes as the camera moves to new regions.
datasets.colorMeaning: orange to red = high carbon dioxide (red is highest); lower amounts are a faint grey or white haze; the globe underneath shows land, ocean and country borders
datasets.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio. Data: DYAMOND GEOS model
